rem:enveloping-algebra:
Remark Universal enveloping algebra. The universal enveloping algebra \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{su}(2)) is the associative algebra generated by e_1,e_2,e_3 subject to the commutation relations. It provides the scaffolding for every finite-dimensional representation of \mathfrak{su}(2) and is the classical limit (q\to 1) of the quantum group \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)).

By the PBW theorem, the monomials \{e_1^{a}e_2^{b}e_3^{c} : a,b,c \geq 0\} form a \mathbb{C}-basis of \mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{su}(2)). In the q-deformed setting, present \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) by generators E, F, K^{\pm 1} over a field k with q \neq 0 and q^2 \neq 1, as \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2). The Groebner--Shirshov resolution of the q-Serre relations shows that the ordered monomials \{F^{c}E^{a}K^{n} : c, a \in \mathbb{N},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\} form a k-basis. When q is not a root of unity, [a]_q!\,[c]_q! \neq 0, so the rescaled monomials F^{(c)}E^{(a)}K^{n} in the Lusztig divided powers E^{(a)} = E^{a}/[a]_q!, F^{(c)} = F^{c}/[c]_q! are again a basis. At a root of unity the divided powers are not defined in this algebra, and the basis is the one in ordinary powers.

This basis provides the explicit coordinates for the fibre algebra \mathrm{SU}_{q_n}(2) at each brane-tower level, and its index set \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{Z} is the same at every level. Flatness of the deformation q \mapsto q_n over the ring of the parameter, which the transition maps in the direct limit \mathcal{A}_\infty = \varinjlim\Gamma(J^1 \mathcal{S}_n, \mathrm{SU}_{q_n}(2)) use, is a stronger statement: the basis theorem is proved for each value of q separately, not over the parameter ring.
def:quantum-su2:
Definition Quantum group \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)). Let q\in\mathbb{C}^{*} with 0<\lvert q\rvert\le 1. The quantum group \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) is the associative \mathbb{C}-algebra generated by E,F,K,K^{-1} subject to:

\begin{align}
  KK^{-1}&=K^{-1}K=1,
    \label{eq:quantum-KK}\\[3pt]
  KEK^{-1}&=q^2E,\quad KFK^{-1}=q^{-2}F,
    \label{eq:quantum-KE}\\[3pt]
  [E,F]&=\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}.
    \label{eq:quantum-EF}
\end{align}
rem:quantum-su2-classical-limit: Remark Classical limit of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)). In the classical limit q\to 1, the generator K of the quantum group reduces to \exp(he_3) and the relations recover the \mathfrak{su}(2) commutation relations of the standard basis.
def:q-casimir:
Definition The q-Casimir element of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)). Let q^2 \neq 1. The q-Casimir element of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) is

  C_q  =  F E  +  \frac{q\,K + q^{-1} K^{-1} - (q + q^{-1})}
                       {(q - q^{-1})^2}.
rem:q-casimir-remark:
Remark Normalisation and role of the q-Casimir element. The q-Casimir element is the distinguished central element of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) whose eigenvalue on the spin-j irreducible encodes the categorical q-angular momentum. Subtracting (q + q^{-1}) in the numerator ensures the eigenvalue vanishes on the trivial representation and has a finite classical limit. Equivalently,

  C_q  =  E F  +  \frac{q^{-1}\,K + q\,K^{-1} - (q + q^{-1})}
                        {(q - q^{-1})^2}.

By existence, C_q is central and acts on the (2j+1)-dimensional highest-weight module V_j as the scalar [j]_q\,[j+1]_q, where [n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1}). Centrality makes C_q an endomorphism of the identity functor on \mathbf{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)), the categorical counterpart of the angular-momentum-squared operator.
prop:q-casimir-classical-limit:
Proposition Classical limit q \to 1 of the q-Casimir eigenvalue. The generic q-Casimir eigenvalue [j]_q\,[j+1]_q is defined over an abstract coefficient field. Its classical limit is the archimedean specialisation to \mathbb{R} at q \to 1.

As q \to 1 in \mathbb{R}, the symmetric q-number converges to its undeformed value:

  \lim_{q \to 1} [n]_q  =  n.

Consequently, the q-Casimir eigenvalue converges to the classical \mathfrak{su}(2) Casimir eigenvalue:

  \lim_{q \to 1} [j]_q\,[j+1]_q  =  j\,(j+1).

The value j(j+1) recovers the classical angular-momentum-squared spectrum. This limit restricts the generic categorical construction to the archimedean side of the algebraic→archimedean wall.
prop:q-casimir-exists:
Proposition Existence of the q-Casimir element. For any ground ring R in which (q - q^{-1}) is invertible, the q-Casimir element

  C_q \;=\; F E + \frac{q  K + q^{-1} K^{-1} - (q + q^{-1})}{(q - q^{-1})^2}

exists as a central element of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) and acts as [j]_q [j+1]_q \mathrm{id} on every simple module V_j.

The existence of the Casimir element is standard quantum-group theory.
prf:q-casimir-exists:
Proof Proof of existence of the q-Casimir element. The formula C_q = FE + (qK + q^{-1}K^{-1} - (q + q^{-1}))/(q - q^{-1})^2 is a well-defined element of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) whenever (q - q^{-1}) is invertible in the ground ring R. Centrality is verified directly using the defining relations of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)): the commutator [E, F] = (K - K^{-1})/(q - q^{-1}) and the K-relations KEK^{-1} = q^2 E, KFK^{-1} = q^{-2} F; the computation is standard (Kassel VI.4).

The eigenvalue on the spin-j irrep is computed by evaluating C_q on the highest-weight vector: K v_j = q^{2j} v_j and E v_j = 0 give C_q v_j = [j]_q[j+1]_q v_j after simplifying the K + K^{-1} term. Hence C_q|_{V_j} = [j]_q[j+1]_q \cdot \mathrm{id}.

Over \mathbb{F}_p, \mathbb{Q}_p, \mathbb{C}_p the same formula holds whenever (q - q^{-1}) is invertible in the base ring — a generic hypothesis excluding roots of unity of small order.
prop:q-casimir-unique:
Proposition Uniqueness of the q-Casimir element up to scalar. The q-Casimir element C_q is the unique central element of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) of the form FE + \phi(K, K^{-1}) whose eigenvalue on the spin-j irrep is [j]_q [j+1]_q. Any two such central elements differ by a scalar multiple of the identity.

This uniqueness result regarding the Joseph--Letzter centre is standard.
prf:q-casimir-unique:
Proof Proof of uniqueness of the q-Casimir element. The centre Z(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))) is a polynomial ring in C_q over the ground ring (Joseph--Letzter, Kassel VI.4.9). Any central element therefore belongs to R[C_q]; in particular, the identity plus a linear term a + b C_q is the only linear-in-C_q central element.

Fixing the eigenvalue on V_j to be [j]_q[j+1]_q (for all j) pins down the coefficient b = 1 and the constant a such that the eigenvalue vanishes on the trivial representation (V_0: [0]_q[1]_q = 0, so a = 0). Hence C_q is unique. Other normalisations (e.g. the non-symmetric q-Casimir C'_q = C_q + \text{const}) differ by a scalar shift, which is absorbed into the ground ring.
prop:r-matrix-braiding-structure:
Proposition Yang--Baxter equation and braid operator from the R-matrix. The universal R-matrix \mathcal{R} \in \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) \hat{\otimes} \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) satisfies the Yang--Baxter equation:

  \mathcal{R}_{12}\mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{23}
  = 
  \mathcal{R}_{23}\mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{12}.

The braid operator \check{R} = P \circ \mathcal{R} (with P the tensor swap) furnishes a representation of the braid group on any tensor product of finite-dimensional \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))-modules.

The underlying R-matrix theory is standard; the eigenvalues q and -q^{-1} (the Hecke channels) provide the tie-in to the physical observable structure.
rem:r-matrix-braiding:
Remark R-matrix and braiding. The R-matrix of \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2)) is the universal element

  \mathcal{R} \in 
  \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))\hat{\otimes}
  \mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))

satisfying the Yang--Baxter equation \mathcal{R}_{12}\mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{23} =\mathcal{R}_{23}\mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{12}. Its action on a tensor product of representations gives the braid operator \check{R}=P\circ\mathcal{R}, furnishing a q-deformed braid group representation that replaces classical twist/flip involutions.
thm:pontryagin-dual-coxeter-character:
Theorem Pontryagin self-duality on abelianised Coxeter group S_n^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2. For every n \geq 2, the abelianisation S_n^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2 of the Coxeter group S_n is canonically Pontryagin self-dual. The character group \widehat{S_n^{\mathrm{ab}}} = \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{C}^\times) is canonically isomorphic to \mathbb{Z}/2 itself via the identification of the unique non-trivial character with the sign homomorphism.

The resulting sign-of-a-permutation observable is the same \mathbb{Z}/2 classified by the bar involution.
prf:pontryagin-dual-coxeter-character:
Proof Proof of pontryagin dual coxeter character. The proof splits into two short verifiable observations:

  1. Self-duality of \mathbb{Z}/2. Every additive homomorphism \varphi \colon \mathbb{Z}/2 \to \mathbb{Z}/2 is determined by its value \varphi(1) \in \mathbb{Z}/2. There are exactly two such values, giving the trivial character and the identity (sign) character. The bijection \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/2) \leftrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/2, \varphi \mapsto \varphi(1), is the canonical self-duality. Composing with the standard embedding \mathbb{Z}/2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}^\times, k \mapsto (-1)^k, identifies \widehat{\mathbb{Z}/2} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2.

  2. Surjectivity of the sign homomorphism \mathrm{sgn} \colon S_n \to \mathbb{Z}/2 for n \geq 2. The transposition \mathrm{swap}(0, 1) \in S_n has sign -1, witnessing the non-trivial sign class. Combined with the identity (trivial class), this realises both elements of \mathbb{Z}/2, so the sign homomorphism is surjective. By the universal property of abelianisation and the fact that S_n for n \geq 2 has abelianisation of order 2 (Coxeter group theory; equivalently, the commutator subgroup is the alternating group A_n), S_n^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2.

Composing (1) and (2): \widehat{S_n^{\mathrm{ab}}} \cong \widehat{\mathbb{Z}/2} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2 \cong S_n^{\mathrm{ab}}, canonically. ∎
sec:lepton-meson-parallel-intro: The torus-knot family T(2,k) and the amphichiral figure-eight knot 4_1 bridge the purely algebraic Hecke quotient of this chapter to the geometric and particle structures of the chapters that follow. Through the Frobenius pairing and Hoefsmit's seminormal representation on H_3(q), the same two-strand and three-strand braid operators that classify leptons also govern meson binding amplitudes, cusp-torus bar parity, and the strong–electromagnetic decomposition of the kaon-to-pion mass ratio.
prop:frobenius-lepton-meson-bridge:
Proposition Frobenius restriction: V_{(2,1)} \!\downarrow_{H_2} = V_{(2)} \oplus V_{(1,1)}. The standard representation V_{(2,1)} of H_3(q) restricts to H_2(q) as the direct sum of its two one-dimensional irreducible representations:

  V_{(2,1)} \big\downarrow_{H_2}
  = V_{(2)} \oplus V_{(1,1)}.

At H_2, the irreps V_{(2)} and V_{(1,1)} are separate. At H_3, they are coupled inside the 2 \times 2 Hoefsmit block of V_{(2,1)}. The off-diagonal element

  b = \sqrt{a_\rho \cdot a_{-\rho} + 1},
  \qquad
  a_\rho = \frac{h}{1 - q^{-2\rho}},

couples the two channels; they decouple exactly when b = 0.

By Frobenius reciprocity:

  \langle \mathrm{Res}(V_{(2,1)}), V_{(2)} \rangle_{H_2}
  = \langle V_{(2,1)}, \mathrm{Ind}(V_{(2)}) \rangle_{H_3}
  = 1.

Each one-dimensional irreducible representation of H_2(q) appears exactly once in the restriction.
prf:frobenius-lepton-meson-bridge:
Proof Proof of frobenius lepton meson bridge. The branching rule H_3 \downarrow H_2 follows from the Pieri / Littlewood–Richardson rule for removing a box from the Young diagram. For each partition \lambda \vdash 3:

  V_{(3)} \downarrow = V_{(2)}, \qquad
  V_{(2,1)} \downarrow = V_{(2)} \oplus V_{(1,1)}, \qquad
  V_{(1^3)} \downarrow = V_{(1,1)}.

The standard representation (2,1) admits removal of a box from either the first row (giving (2)) or the second row (giving (1,1)), hence the two-term decomposition. \square
rem:frobenius-lepton-meson-bridge-interp:
Remark Mathematical novelty of the lepton–meson bridge. The underlying branching rule V_{(2,1)} \downarrow V_{(2)} \oplus V_{(1,1)} is standard representation theory. The mathematical novelty lies in applying it topologically: mapping the physical entanglement of lepton channels directly to the mass-carrying partition of the meson sector.

In this reading the meson sector's sole mass-carrying partition is this entangled lepton spectrum. When b = 0, the meson reverts to two independent leptons; when b \ne 0, the channels mix, producing Hopf link binding. The branching then supports three readings:

  1. The lepton mass ratio m_\mu / m_\mathfrak{e} measures the separated V_{(2)} \leftrightarrow V_{(1,1)} transition.
  2. The meson mass ratio m_K / m_\pi measures the same transition inside the entangled (2,1) block.
  3. The Hoefsmit off-diagonal b is the amplitude at which the lepton pair-channel becomes the meson binding channel.

This branching explains why charge conjugation C aligns with the bar involution at H_2 (separate 1-dim irreps) but diverges at H_3 (entangled 2-dim irrep with off-diagonal b).
prop:hoefsmit-binding-amplitude:
Proposition Hoefsmit binding amplitude b^2 = [3]_q / [2]_q^2. The off-diagonal element b of the Hoefsmit seminormal matrix for the standard representation (2,1) of H_3(q) satisfies:

  b^2 = \frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^2},
  \qquad
  1 - b^2 = \frac{1}{[2]_q^2}.

These identities hold exactly for every q with q^4 \neq 1, the condition under which the seminormal entries a_{\pm 2} = h/(1 - q^{\mp 4}) are defined; they do not depend on the aether parameter. Stated in terms of [2]_q alone, the identity needs only [2]_q \neq 0.
prf:hoefsmit-binding-amplitude:
Proof Proof of hoefsmit binding amplitude. The Hoefsmit seminormal matrix for \sigma_2 on V_{(2,1)} has a 2 \times 2 block with entries

  a_\rho = \frac{h}{1 - q^{-2\rho}},
  \qquad
  a_{-\rho} = \frac{h}{1 - q^{2\rho}},
  \qquad
  b = \sqrt{a_\rho \cdot a_{-\rho} + 1},

where \rho = 2 is the axial distance and h = q - q^{-1}. The product of the diagonal entries is

  a_\rho \cdot a_{-\rho}
  = \frac{h^2}{(1 - q^{-4})(1 - q^4)}
  = \frac{h^2}{-(h^2)(h^2 + 4)}
  = -\frac{1}{h^2 + 4}
  = -\frac{1}{[2]_q^2}.

Therefore b^2 = -1/[2]_q^2 + 1 = ([2]_q^2 - 1)/[2]_q^2. Since [2]_q^2 = (q + q^{-1})^2 = h^2 + 4 and [3]_q = q^2 + 1 + q^{-2} = h^2 + 3 = [2]_q^2 - 1:

  b^2 = \frac{[2]_q^2 - 1}{[2]_q^2} = \frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^2}.
  \qquad\square
rem:hoefsmit-binding-amplitude-pion-read:
Remark The binding amplitude and the pion decay energy. Read physically, through the Hoefsmit identities, the pion decay \pi \to \mu + \nu de-entangles the meson into V_{(2)} \oplus V_{(1,1)}. It releases a fraction 1 - b^2 = 1/[2]_q^2 of the pion's rest energy:

  E_{\mathrm{bind}} = \frac{m_\pi}{[2]_q^2}.

The residual energy m_\pi \cdot b^2 flows into the de-entangled lepton channel V_{(2)}.

The identification of 1 - b^2 with a fraction of the pion's rest energy is an interpretation; the proposition proves only the two identities.
prop:hoefsmit-toroidal-ladder-locus:
Proposition Toroidal locus of the Hoefsmit mixing ladder: (n,\mu) = (d - \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}) is forced. Let R be a field of characteristic zero and let \alpha, \beta \in R be constants. If the associated-Legendre order-ladder factor at degree n = d + \alpha and order \mu = \beta reproduces the squared Hoefsmit channel-mixing numerator identically in the axial distance d,

(d + \alpha - \beta)(d + \alpha + \beta + 1) \;=\; d^2 - 1
\qquad \text{for all } d \in R,

then

\alpha = -\tfrac{1}{2},
\qquad
\beta \in \bigl\{ \tfrac{1}{2},\; -\tfrac{3}{2} \bigr\},

i.e. (n, \mu) = \bigl(d - \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr) up to the Legendre reflection \mu \mapsto -\mu - 1. The half-integer degree shift — the signature of the toroidal harmonic family P^\mu_{\nu - 1/2} — is forced by the Hoefsmit mixing structure, not imposed.

Context

The Hoefsmit seminormal block at axial distance d mixes the two lepton channels with amplitude b satisfying b^2 = [d-1]_q [d+1]_q / [d]_q^2 (prop:hoefsmit-binding-amplitude is the d = 2 meson case b^2 = [3]_q/[2]_q^2). At q \to 1 the squared mixing numerator is d^2 - 1. The associated-Legendre order-ladder factor is (n - \mu)(n + \mu + 1), and the toroidal harmonics — the separated eigenfunctions around a vortex ring [lebedev1965] — are exactly the Legendre family at half-integer degree \nu - \tfrac{1}{2} [whipple1917]. The proposition says the match between the two structures admits no freedom: the degree shift -\tfrac{1}{2} and the order \tfrac{1}{2} are the unique solution.

Because the q-bracket identity [d-1]_q[d+1]_q = [d]_q^2 - 1 holds for all q, the same forcing computation runs verbatim at the q-deformed level (the coefficient matching gives q^{2\alpha + 1} = 1); the half-integer shift survives q-deformation. The q-layer statement has been verified by direct computation.

The physical reading: the two windings (\mu, \nu) of a toroidal harmonic P^\mu_{\nu-1/2}(\cosh\eta)\, e^{i\mu\theta} e^{i\nu\varphi} are the two local one-dimensional channel oscillations of a bound vortex pair, and the forced -\tfrac{1}{2} is the zero-point offset of the interpolating channel ladder.
prf:hoefsmit-toroidal-ladder-locus:
Proof Proof of the toroidal ladder locus. Expanding the ladder factor,

(d + \alpha - \beta)(d + \alpha + \beta + 1)
= d^2 + (2\alpha + 1)\, d + (\alpha - \beta)(\alpha + \beta + 1).

Equality with d^2 - 1 for all d matches coefficients: the linear coefficient gives 2\alpha + 1 = 0, so \alpha = -\tfrac{1}{2} (characteristic zero); the constant coefficient then gives

\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2} - \beta\bigr)\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2} + \beta\bigr) = -1
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\bigl(\beta + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)^2 = 1
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\bigl(\beta - \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)\bigl(\beta + \tfrac{3}{2}\bigr) = 0,

so \beta = \tfrac{1}{2} or \beta = -\tfrac{3}{2}. In a field the product vanishes only if a factor does, giving the two stated solutions, which are exchanged by the Legendre reflection \mu \mapsto -\mu - 1 about \mu = -\tfrac{1}{2}. The validity direction is the polynomial identity (d - 1)(d + 1) = d^2 - 1. \blacksquare
prop:three-strand-color-winding-rigidity:
Proposition Rigidity of the three-strand color winding: (\sigma_1\sigma_2)^3 = \mathrm{Id} on the (2,1) block, q-independently. On the 2-dimensional (2,1) Hoefsmit block of H_3(q), the uniform three-strand rotation M = \rho_{(2,1)}(\sigma_1\sigma_2) has

\mathrm{tr}\,M = -1, \qquad \det M = 1, \qquad M^3 = \mathrm{Id},

for every q with 1 - q^4 invertible. The eigenvalues of M are the primitive cube roots of unity, independently of q.

The proof is Cayley–Hamilton: trace -1 and determinant 1 give the \zeta_3 quadratic M^2 = -M - 1, hence M^3 = \mathrm{Id}. The trace identity is a Laurent identity in q alone; the determinant identity is exactly the Hoefsmit constraint \beta^2 = a_2 a_{-2} + 1 on the binding amplitude (prop:hoefsmit-binding-amplitude). Both hold over a generic commutative ring with q a unit and with both \beta and the axial entry a_{-2} carried as constrained variables — \beta^2 = a_{-2} a_2 + 1 and a_{-2} (1 - q^4) = q - q^{-1} — so neither the square root nor the axial-distance quotient appears (no division, no \mathbb{R}), and the cube identity follows from the two scalar facts. The hypothesis 1 - q^4 invertible is what makes the axial entry a_{-2} = (q - q^{-1})/(1 - q^4) of the Hoefsmit block defined. With a_{-2} carried as a constrained variable, the argument needs only 1 - q^2 invertible and only for the trace; the statement's hypothesis implies it. At q^2 = 1 the defining relation for a_{-2} degenerates and constrains nothing. The determinant identity needs no hypothesis at all.

Since the closures of (\sigma_1\sigma_2)^k are the (3,k) torus links, the proposition says the compact winding of the three-strand torus-link tower is topological: a \zeta_3 (color/triality) rotation that does not flow with the aether modulus, in contrast to the modulus-carrying hyperbolic winding pair q^{\pm 2k} of the 1-dimensional channels. The level-lattice and vortex readings — winding pair (k,\ k \bmod 3) for the three-strand (Borromean/nucleon) carrier, and the alternating-word deformation of the same rotation — are developed in the channel- interpolation cross-check and its witnesses (toroidal-level-selection-three-strand-probe, alternating-tower-borromean-winding-probe).
prf:three-strand-color-winding-rigidity:
Proof Proof of the color-winding rigidity. Write M = \rho_{(2,1)}(\sigma_1)\,\rho_{(2,1)}(\sigma_2) with \rho_{(2,1)}(\sigma_1) = \mathrm{diag}(q, -q^{-1}) and the axial-distance-2 Hoefsmit block for \sigma_2, so that

M = \begin{pmatrix} q\,a_{-2} & q\,\beta \\ -q^{-1}\beta & -q^{-1} a_{2} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
a_{\pm 2} = \frac{q - q^{-1}}{1 - q^{\mp 4}},
\qquad
\beta^2 = a_2 a_{-2} + 1 .

Two scalar computations. Trace: using q\,a_{-2} = (q^2-1)/(1-q^4) and q^{-1} a_2 = q^2(q^2-1)/(q^4-1),

\mathrm{tr}\, M
= \frac{(q^2-1)(1+q^2)}{1-q^4}
= \frac{q^4-1}{1-q^4} = -1,

a rational identity in q alone (denominators nonzero since q^4 \neq 1). Determinant: \det M = (q\,a_{-2})(-q^{-1}a_2) - (q\beta)(-q^{-1}\beta) = \beta^2 - a_2 a_{-2} = 1, which is exactly the Hoefsmit constraint on \beta.

By Cayley–Hamilton for a 2\times 2 matrix, M^2 - (\mathrm{tr}\,M)\,M + (\det M)\,\mathrm{Id} = 0, so M^2 = -M - \mathrm{Id} (the \zeta_3 quadratic), and multiplying by M:

M^3 = -M^2 - M = (M + \mathrm{Id}) - M = \mathrm{Id}. \qquad \blacksquare

Neither the trace nor the determinant identity involves q beyond the nonvanishing conditions, so the conclusion holds for every q with q^4 \neq 1: the eigenvalues of M are the primitive cube roots of unity at every q — the color winding is rigid.
prop:self-dual-higgs-real-volume:
Proposition The self-dual Higgs (4_1) has a real complex volume (\mathrm{CS}=0). The figure-eight knot 4_1 (the Higgs mass-scale motif) is strongly amphichiral, as tabulated by Dale Rolfsen [rolfsen] and analysed in complex Chern--Simons theory by Edward Witten [witten2011, §5.3]. Under the bar-involution \sigma\colon q \mapsto q^{-1}, its colored Jones polynomial is fixed:

  J_N(4_1; q) = J_N(4_1; q^{-1}) \qquad (\forall N).

Consequently, its Neumann--Zagier complex volume \mathbb{V}(4_1) = \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) + i\,\mathrm{CS}(4_1) of Walter D. Neumann and Don Zagier [neumann-zagier1985] (in the asymptotic colored-Jones normalisation of Rinat M. Kashaev [kashaev1997] and Hitoshi Murakami and Jun Murakami [murakami-murakami2001]) is real:

  \mathrm{CS}(4_1) = 0,
  \qquad
  \mathrm{Re}\,\mathbb{V}(4_1) = \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) \approx 2.0299.

The bare Higgs knot contributes only the real volume (mass) face. Its imaginary (decay) face vanishes, proving that \mathfrak{Q}_\beta is not a property of the lone Higgs knot.

For the amphichiral 4_1, its invariant trace field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}) and invariant quaternion algebra are closed under complex conjugation by the necessary amphicheirality criterion of Walter D. Neumann and Alan W. Reid [neumann-reid, §3.2, Prop. 3.4], and both archimedean saddles (hyperbolic and torus) collapse onto the real axis. This self-duality is an algebraic identity over any commutative ring with a bar-involution.
prop:cusp-shape-bar-parity:
Proposition Cusp-shape bar-parity: the figure-eight modulus splits as \mathfrak{V} = \mathrm{Vol} + i\,\mathrm{CS}. The cusp shape of the figure-eight knot 4_1 is \omega = e^{i\pi/3}, a primitive sixth root of unity — the root of the cyclotomic polynomial \Phi_6(z) = z^2 - z + 1 in the upper half-plane, with trace field \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3}) [neumann-reid]. Split \omega along the bar-involution \sigma\colon x \mapsto x^{-1} into its symmetric and antisymmetric shapes:

  \mathrm{barEven}(x) = x + x^{-1}, \qquad \mathrm{barOdd}(x) = x - x^{-1}.

Then the cusp shape realizes the two faces of the Neumann–Zagier complex volume \mathfrak{V} = \mathrm{Vol} + i\,\mathrm{CS}:

  \mathrm{barEven}(\omega) = 1, \qquad \mathrm{barOdd}(\omega)^2 = -3.

The bar-even part is the rational Volume normalization 2\cos(\pi/3) = 1; the bar-odd part is the \sqrt{-3} Chern–Simons modulus (2i\sin(\pi/3))^2 = -3.

The identity holds over any field carrying a root of \Phi_6. From \omega^2 - \omega + 1 = 0 one gets \omega^{-1} = 1 - \omega (since \omega(1-\omega) = 1), whence

  \mathrm{barEven}(\omega) = \omega + (1 - \omega) = 1,
  \qquad
  \mathrm{barOdd}(\omega) = 2\omega - 1,

and (2\omega - 1)^2 = 4\omega^2 - 4\omega + 1 = -3 using \omega^2 = \omega - 1. The computation uses only field operations over a generic field (no archimedean structure).

On the name "cusp shape". In the literature the cusp shape of a hyperbolic 3-manifold with one torus cusp is the similarity class of the Euclidean structure induced on a horospherical cross-section of the cusp, that is a point of the Teichmüller space of the torus [dang-purcell, §1, §3]. In the holonomy normalisation \mu \mapsto \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}, \lambda \mapsto \begin{pmatrix}-1&c\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} it is the ratio c of the longitude and meridian translations, which depends on the chosen basis of \pi_1(T^2) up to an integral Möbius transformation [dubois2007, §3.3]. The number \omega = e^{i\pi/3} used above is a different object: it is the shape parameter of each of the two regular ideal tetrahedra into which the figure-eight complement decomposes. The identities \mathrm{barEven}(\omega) = 1 and \mathrm{barOdd}(\omega)^2 = -3 are statements about that primitive sixth root of unity and hold as stated; the phrase "cusp shape of 4_1" in this block refers to the tetrahedral shape parameter, not to the cusp-torus modulus c, and the two should not be identified when either is cited.
prop:meridian-holonomy-boost:
Proposition Meridian holonomy is a boost: \mathrm{barEven}(q)^2 - \mathrm{barOdd}(q)^2 = 4. The meridian holonomy of the cusp torus is multiplication by the aether parameter q: one meridian turn is one application of the R-matrix — one crossing, one knot operation. Under the bar-split of the cusp shape, this holonomy satisfies the boost identity

  \mathrm{barEven}(q)^2 - \mathrm{barOdd}(q)^2 = 4 \qquad (q \neq 0),

the \cosh^2 - \sinh^2 = 1 relation (\times 4): the holonomy lies on a hyperbola, so one meridian turn is a hyperbolic rotation, not a compact spin.

Moreover, composing turns multiplies the holonomies q \mapsto q\,q', and this adds rapidity: the bar-parity shapes obey the addition laws

  2\,\mathrm{barEven}(q\,q') = \mathrm{barEven}(q)\,\mathrm{barEven}(q') + \mathrm{barOdd}(q)\,\mathrm{barOdd}(q'),
  2\,\mathrm{barOdd}(q\,q') = \mathrm{barOdd}(q)\,\mathrm{barEven}(q') + \mathrm{barEven}(q)\,\mathrm{barOdd}(q').

Additive rapidity corresponds to multiplicative holonomy — the boost group law. All three identities hold over a generic field. At a real aether q_0 > 1 the turn is a genuine boost of rapidity \ln q_0; only at a root of unity (\lvert q \rvert = 1) is it a compact U(1) spin.
rem:meridian-exceptional-divisor-note:
Remark The meridian is at the exceptional divisor; the per-operation tick is the Compton time, not the Planck time. Physically, the meridian is a 1-cycle in the exceptional-divisor fibre \mathcal{S}_p: after the base coordinate hits the discriminant and the smooth base pinches, the cusp torus and its meridian are the geometry of \mathcal{S}_p. So the statement "the meridian is at the exceptional divisor" is literal, and by the boost identity one meridian turn — one knot operation — is a hyperbolic rotation of rapidity \ln q_0 \approx 0.104 along the bar-odd (Chern–Simons) axis, the same axis along which the cusp shape sits (\mathrm{barOdd}(\omega)^2 = -3).

This fixes the natural time per operation, and it is not the Planck time. A rotation is dimensionless; converting it to a duration divides by an energy, t = \hbar / E, and the aether energy scale is m_e (the leptonic calibration CAL-1). The per-operation tick is therefore the electron Compton time

  t_C = \hbar / (m_e c^2) \approx 1.29 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{s},

which is \sim 22 orders of magnitude longer than the Planck time t_P \approx 5.39 \times 10^{-44} s. The ratio is exactly m_{\mathrm{Planck}} / m_e \approx 2.4 \times 10^{22} — the gravitational hierarchy, a standard measured quantity built from \hbar, c, G, m_e and owing nothing to this framework.

Identifying the computational tick with the Planck time would pin the aether at m_{\mathrm{Planck}}, i.e. introduce Newton's constant G — an input outside the three-calibration weak sector (m_e, P_{\mathrm{skew}}^{\beta}, P_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\pi}). That is a fourth calibration and an aether-scale derivation, which the framework does not undertake. The honest per-operation tick is the Compton / electroweak time; the 22-order gap to gravity is not something the framework predicts, and by construction it need not.
prop:winding-lattice-norm-form:
Proposition The winding lattice of a braid-word geodesic: \mathrm{Im}\,\mathfrak{V}_{4_1} is the norm form of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt3]. A closed geodesic on the cusp torus of the figure-eight knot — the path traced by a braid word's particle/vortex flow — is a class (m, \ell) in the cusp lattice \mathbb{Z}\langle 1, \omega\rangle, where m counts meridian turns, \ell counts longitude turns, and \omega = e^{i\pi/3} is the cusp shape (Cusp-shape bar-parity: the figure-eight modulus splits as \mathfrak{V} = \mathrm{Vol} + i\,\mathrm{CS}). Since one meridian turn is a boost of rapidity \ln q_0 (Meridian holonomy is a boost: \mathrm{barEven}(q)^2 - \mathrm{barOdd}(q)^2 = 4), the geodesic's log-holonomy is

  u_{m,\ell} = (\ln q_0)\,(m + \ell\,\omega).

Let s satisfy s^2 = 3 and write \omega = (1+s)/2. For every c, m, \ell in a commutative ring,

  \bigl(c(2m+\ell)\bigr)^2 - \bigl(c\,\ell\,s\bigr)^2 = c^2\bigl[(2m+\ell)^2 - 3\ell^2\bigr].

The bracket is the norm form of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt3], of discriminant 12. Moreover the two relevant quadratic orders behave oppositely under their fundamental units:

  1. (silver, disc 12) \ N(2+\sqrt3) = +1, and every power satisfies x_n^2 - 3y_n^2 = +1;
  2. (golden, disc 5) \ N(\varphi) = -1 for \varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2, and N(\varphi^n) = (-1)^n.

Since 2\,\mathrm{Re}\,u_{m,\ell} = (\ln q_0)(2m+\ell) and 2\,\mathrm{Im}\,u_{m,\ell} = (\ln q_0)\,\ell\sqrt3, the identity says the indefinite pairing \mathrm{Re}^2 - \mathrm{Im}^2 on the cusp lattice is the disc-12 norm form. Combined with the imaginary part of the Neumann–Zagier complex volume, \mathrm{Im}\,\mathfrak{V}_{4_1} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\bigl(\mathrm{Re}^2 u - \mathrm{Im}^2 u\bigr), this gives

  \mathrm{Im}\,\mathfrak{V}_{4_1}(u_{m,\ell}) = \frac{\sqrt3}{16}\,(\ln q_0)^2\,\bigl[(2m+\ell)^2 - 3\ell^2\bigr],

so the sign of \mathrm{Im}\,\mathfrak{V}_{4_1} is a discrete arithmetic invariant of the winding class alone, carrying no dependence on q_0.

Two consequences are immediate. First, because \sqrt3 is irrational the form never vanishes on a nonzero lattice class: every geodesic is strictly boost-dominated (>0) or spin-dominated (<0), never null. The spin-dominated sector is the winding-slope window m/\ell \in \bigl(-\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\, -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigr), containing exactly the integer slopes 0 and -1 — the longitude-dominated directions. The meridian (1,0) gives +4 and the longitude (0,1) gives -2.

Second, the level set (2m+\ell)^2 - 3\ell^2 = 1 is Pell's equation, whose solutions are the units (2+\sqrt3)^n. Writing x_n + y_n\sqrt3 = (2+\sqrt3)^n gives x_n = \cosh(n\rho) and \sqrt3\,y_n = \sinh(n\rho) with \rho = \mathrm{arccosh}\,2 = \ln(2+\sqrt3), and under (\mathrm{barEven}, \mathrm{barOdd}) = (2x_n, 2\sqrt3\,y_n) this is exactly the boost hyperbola \mathrm{barEven}^2 - \mathrm{barOdd}^2 = 4 of Meridian holonomy is a boost: \mathrm{barEven}(q)^2 - \mathrm{barOdd}(q)^2 = 4. The boost identity and Pell's equation are the same statement, and the integer solutions form a discrete boost subgroup of rapidity n\,\rho.

The contrast in items 1 and 2 is what distinguishes the two orders. The silver recursion (a,b) \mapsto (2a+3b,\, a+2b) preserves a^2 - 3b^2; the golden recursion (a,b) \mapsto (b,\, a+b) negates a^2 + ab - b^2. Each is a single polynomial identity. Hence a sign alternating with a winding exponent is structurally unavailable on the cusp-torus order and available on the golden order carried by Bring's surface.

The ring identity holds over a generic commutative ring (no ordering, no \mathbb{R}, s entering only through s^2 = 3), the two norm recursions hold over \mathbb{Z}, and induction gives N(\varphi^n) = (-1)^n.
rem:winding-parity-sign-transport:
Remark Winding parity as a sign mechanism: what the golden order would buy, and why it is not yet a derivation. The two quadratic orders of The winding lattice of a braid-word geodesic suggest a reading of the sign carried by the S-channel, which this remark states and then bounds.

The canonical braid words of the fundamental knots are powers of the half-figure-eight word w = \sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1}: the figure-eight is 4_1 = w^2 and the Borromean rings are L6a4 = w^3 (fundamental-knots-operator-basis). Reading the exponent n as the winding number of the associated geodesic, the golden order's alternating norm N(\varphi^n) = (-1)^n assigns a sign to each knot by the parity of n alone:

  4_1 = w^2 \ (n \text{ even}) \ \longmapsto\ +, \qquad
  L6a4 = w^3 \ (n \text{ odd}) \ \longmapsto\ -.

Both match the observed signs at the corresponding anchors, with no free parameter. The rule is parameter-free in a strong sense: nothing in it refers to q_0, so it is insensitive to the \sim 10^{-8} separation between the two anchor moduli. This is the structural interest of the reading — a sign difference between two knots need not be produced by a hypersensitive function of q_0 at all, if it is produced by their winding parity instead.

The bar-parity split displays the same parity as a channel exchange. For x = \varphi^n the split of Cusp-shape bar-parity: the figure-eight modulus splits as \mathfrak{V} = \mathrm{Vol} + i\,\mathrm{CS} gives \mathrm{barEven}(x) = x + x^{-1} and \mathrm{barOdd}(x) = x - x^{-1}, and which of the two integer sequences L_n and F_n\sqrt5 realizes the \cosh and which the \sinh exchanges with the parity of n:

  n \text{ even}: (\mathrm{barEven}, \mathrm{barOdd}) = (L_n,\, F_n\sqrt5),
  \qquad
  n \text{ odd}: (\mathrm{barEven}, \mathrm{barOdd}) = (F_n\sqrt5,\, L_n),

both satisfying \mathrm{barEven}^2 - \mathrm{barOdd}^2 = 4. The even and odd channels are exchanged by the parity of the winding, which is the same datum that flips the norm.

Scope. Two limitations are essential.

First, the identification of the S-channel sign with \mathrm{Im}\,\mathfrak{V} is derived on the cusp torus, where the relevant order is the silver one, of discriminant 12. There the norm of every unit power is +1, so no parity flip exists; the sign there is carried by the winding slope, not the winding parity. Transporting the mechanism to the golden order requires the corresponding complex-volume computation on Bring's surface, which is not carried out. The parity reading is therefore an analogy supported by two sign agreements — a conjectural mechanism, not a derivation.

Second, the magnitudes are not accounted for. Since \lvert N(\varphi^n)\rvert = 1 for every n, the parity rule alone predicts equal magnitudes at the two anchors, whereas the observed ratio is about 4.08; the closest natural golden candidate, \varphi^3 \approx 4.236, misses by roughly 4\%. No winding pair is selected to close that gap. The reason for the restraint is structural rather than tactical: Dang and Purcell show that cusp shapes of tunnel-number-one manifolds are dense in the Teichmüller space of the torus, so for a general cusp shape \tau the form becomes (m + \ell\tau_1)^2 - \ell^2\tau_2^2 and a knot may be chosen to realize essentially any desired value. Selecting a knot or a winding pair to reproduce a magnitude would therefore be unconstrained curve-fitting, and the agreement it produced would carry no evidential weight.

What survives is narrow: the sign is available from arithmetic rather than from sensitivity to q_0, and of the two orders in play only the golden one can supply it.
prop:meson-em-sinh-closed-form:
Proposition Meson EM sinh-channel closed-form 1 + \hbar_q - \hbar_q^2/2 = (3q^2 - 1)/(2q^2). Let R be a commutative ring in which 2 is invertible, and let q \in R^\times. Writing the aether Planck quantum \hbar_q = (q - 1)/q,

  1 + \hbar_q - \hbar_q^2/2
  \;=\;
  1 + \frac{1 - q^{-2}}{2}
  \;=\;
  \frac{3 - q^{-2}}{2}
  \;=\;
  \frac{3 q^2 - 1}{2 q^2}.

What this proposition claims, and what it does not. The displayed chain is an exact identity of rational functions over R, and that is its entire content. It says that two spellings of one quantity agree. It does not identify that quantity with any physical correction, and it must not be cited as though it did.
prf:meson-em-sinh-closed-form:
Proof Proof of meson em sinh closed form. The four expressions are equal as rational functions of q over any commutative ring in which q and 2 are invertible (the factor \tfrac12 needs 2 invertible, so characteristic 2 is excluded). Starting from the leftmost, expand \hbar_q^2 = (1 - q^{-1})^2 = 1 - 2 q^{-1} + q^{-2}, so

  1 + \hbar_q - \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar_q^2
  = 1 + (1 - q^{-1}) - \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - 2 q^{-1} + q^{-2})
  = \tfrac{3}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2} q^{-2}
  = \frac{3 - q^{-2}}{2}.

Multiplying numerator and denominator by q^2 gives (3 q^2 - 1)/(2 q^2). \square
rem:meson-em-sinh-ratio-reading:
Remark The meson mass ratio and its electromagnetic factor. The meson ratio. The mass-squared ratio is:

  \frac{m_K^2}{m_\pi^2}
  \;=\;
  [3]_q \cdot [4]_q
  \;+\;
  \frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{em}}}{\pi}
  \cdot
  \bigl(1 + \log(1 + \hbar_q)\bigr).

The strong fusion [3]_q \cdot [4]_q is framework-derived and proved; it supplies \approx 99.98\% of the ratio, and the electromagnetic term is a \approx 203 ppm correction.

The electromagnetic factor is the full series, not the second-order truncation. Reading the rational expression \tfrac{3q^2-1}{2q^2} of this proposition directly as the physical electromagnetic correction would replace the full logarithmic factor 1 + \log(1+\hbar_q) by its quadratic Taylor polynomial 1 + \hbar_q - \hbar_q^2/2. Where a convergent power series is truncated is an external choice; writing the truncated sum in rational closed form conceals that choice rather than deriving it.

The stopping order was chosen against the data. Evaluated at the aether anchor, the error in m_K/m_\pi against the measured value is 479.1, 23.4, 53.5, 51.3, 51.49, 51.474, 51.4755 parts per billion for the series stopped at \hbar_q^1, \dots, \hbar_q^7, converging to 51.4754 parts per billion. The second order is the only order that falls below the limit the series converges to, and every subsequent term moves away from the measurement. A convergent series does not produce a single outlying term; selection does.

Removing the truncation moves the prediction from 23.45 to 51.48 parts per billion, against a target of 263.6. The prediction survives with a margin of 5.1, so nothing downstream turns on the choice.

Scope of the \alpha_{\mathrm{em}} input. The \alpha_{\mathrm{em}} entering the electromagnetic term is the framework's own derived value — the bare force-carrier coupling dressed by the Chern--Simons tower, \alpha_{\mathrm{em}}^{-1} \approx 137.0359351. No measured constant is imported.

The distinction between the derived and the bare coupling matters. Substituting the bare coupling q\,[9]_q\,[10]_q \approx 136.82 (the order-zero term) degrades m_K^2/m_\pi^2 to \approx 363 parts per billion; at every order from one upward, including the exact resummation, the deviation is \approx 47 parts per billion. The agreement is therefore not \alpha_{\mathrm{em}}-anchored.

The ratio is not, however, parameter-free. Two inputs remain selected. The pair (3,4) in [3]_q \cdot [4]_q was found by scanning products of q-integers, and the derivation of that pair from the braid content is open. And \alpha_{\mathrm{em}}, though derived rather than imported, is derived conditionally: its Chern--Simons dressing rests on a Witten \kappa Gram-determinant value that carries an open sorry. The strong core alone misses the target by a factor of 385, so the correction that clears it inherits that condition.
prop:meson-qcg-fusion-identity:
Proposition q-Clebsch–Gordan fusion identity [3]_q\cdot[4]_q = [2]_q + [4]_q + [6]_q. The q-integers satisfy the q-Clebsch–Gordan fusion identity:

  [3]_q \cdot [4]_q \;=\; [2]_q + [4]_q + [6]_q.
prf:meson-qcg-fusion-identity:
Proof Proof of meson qcg fusion identity. Using [n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1}), multiply both sides by (q - q^{-1})^2 to clear denominators. The identity becomes the ring identity

  (q^3 - q^{-3})(q^4 - q^{-4})
  \;=\;
  (q - q^{-1}) \cdot
  \bigl((q^2 - q^{-2}) + (q^4 - q^{-4}) + (q^6 - q^{-6})\bigr),

which holds in any field with q \ne 0 by direct expansion. \square
rem:meson-qcg-fusion-identity-mass-readi: Remark The fusion identity and the meson mass-squared ratio. The fusion identity is used as the categorical foundation for the meson mass-squared ratio m_K^2 / m_\pi^2. Since a meson is a 2-body state, its mass-squared is a bilinear quantity evaluated on the pair. The comparison of this ratio with measurement is made in the meson ratio remark.
sec:q-difference-viewpoint-method:
Several framework quantities—the \mathfrak{Q}_\beta element, the \alpha_{EM} factor, and the Markov trace—are analysed via the q-difference shift \sigma_q : q \mapsto q\zeta at roots of unity.

A Habiro-type element satisfies a q-difference equation (1 - \sigma_q)\,F = \delta\,(q;q)_\infty. This shift is diagonalised by the Fourier transform over \langle\zeta\rangle. Because the q-Pochhammer vanishes at primitive roots of unity, evaluating the expansion truncates the sum to an exact, finite spectrum. When F is rational, solving the equation reduces to partial-fraction decomposition.

This fibre-level viewpoint keeps q formal. The operative symmetry is the bar involution q \mapsto q^{-1}, not a reality assumption.
prop:alpha-em-habiro-bar-involution:
Proposition The \alpha_{EM} Habiro element [2]_q(1-h^2\alpha) is a bar-involution fixed point, with H(1)=2, H(-1)=-2. Let H(q) = [2]_q\,(1 - h^2\alpha) be the \alpha_{EM} Habiro element.

  1. H is a fixed point of the bar involution: H(q^{-1}) = H(q).
  2. Its leading special values are H(1) = 2 and H(-1) = -2.

These fibre-level statements place H entirely in the charge-conjugation-symmetric sector. The lowest root-of-unity evaluation H(\zeta_1) = 2 supplies the classical leading term for \alpha/(4\pi). The exact modular zero H(\zeta_4) = 0 is the structural dual of the \mathfrak{Q}_\beta modular pole.
prop:figure-eight-reeb-rotation:
Proposition The figure-eight knot operator acts unitarily on V_{(2,1)}. Let \varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2. For every real q with \varphi^{-1} < q < \varphi, the figure-eight knot operator M_{4_1} = (\sigma_1\sigma_2^{-1})^2, acting on V_{(2,1)}, has eigenvalues of unit modulus:

  \lambda_{4_1} = e^{\pm i\theta},
  \qquad |\lambda_{4_1}| = 1.

Its reading as a q-Reeb rotation angle is given in rem:figure-eight-reeb-rotation-reeb-reading.

At the endpoints q \in \{\varphi^{-1}, \varphi\} the eigenvalue is 1, and for q > \varphi or 0 < q < \varphi^{-1} the eigenvalues are real and not of unit modulus.
